idiom_name: explicit idempotent release method + ownership-aware cascade (finalizer only as backstop)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: the owner exposes one canonical release operation (Close()/Dispose()) that (1) is idempotent - the second call is a no-op, (2) releases exactly the resources it acquired, cascading to owned sub-resources in reverse acquisition order, (3) never releases borrowed resources, and (4) records the disposed state so later use fails fast instead of operating on a released handle. Provide a scope-bound call-site mechanism wherever the language has one (using, with, try-with-resources, Using, defer, RAII) so every exit path releases; keep any finalizer or cleaner strictly as a safety net for unmanaged resources, suppressed after an explicit release. Where release can fail, split the observable operation (a Close() that can throw) from the destructor/finalizer path (no-throw). In Python, prefer @contextmanager or contextlib.contextmanager for generator-based context managers; in Java prefer try-with-resources over manual try/finally; in C# prefer using declarations (C# 8+) over using statements for clearer scope binding.
code_sketch:
owner = acquire()             # owns exactly the resources it created
begin scope:                  # with/using/try-with-resources/defer/RAII
    owner.use()
end scope:                    # runs on every exit path
    owner.close()             # idempotent: second close is a no-op
# close() releases owned resources in reverse order; borrowed ones stay with
# their owner; any use() after close() raises instead of touching a dead handle
pitfalls: A release operation that does nothing while the object stays usable turns every later call into undefined behaviour; either fail fast or keep the object valid.
Without a documented ownership rule, two owners dispose the same handle or neither does; borrowed references need a non-owning wrapper.
Asking a finalizer to do the real cleanup reintroduces non-deterministic release and hides the missing dispose call.

Throwing from Dispose masks the original exception in C#; Java's try-with-resources attaches the close exception as suppressed. Always prefer non-throwing cleanup paths in finalizer/dispose-calling-dispose.
Single-use context managers (Python @contextmanager-decorated generators) cannot be reused across multiple with statements; attempting reuse raises RuntimeError.

Wrong move: implementing IDisposable/AutoCloseable on any object with interesting scoped behavior (locks, transaction or audit-context markers) because `using` is convenient -> readers can no longer tell genuine resource owners from scoping sugar and skip disposing the ones that matter -> implement the protocol only when the object owns something the GC cannot reclaim; use try/finally or a dedicated scope helper for pure state restoration.

Wrong move: registering a Java Cleaner (or finalizer) whose cleaning action captures `this`, or adding one to every type 'just in case' -> the owner never becomes phantom-reachable so the action never runs, or every allocation pays finalization overhead -> keep cleanup state in a static class or record that never references the owner, and attach cleaners only where unmanaged memory exists.

Wrong move: letting pooled or leased resources (DB connections, WCF/channel proxies) fall back to GC for release -> the pool starves under load and, on faulted proxies, Dispose throws and masks the original operation exception -> make dispose the only return-to-pool path, wrap every lease in the scope construct, and swallow-or-log inside Dispose on known faulted states.
